extracted.intended_audience: general readers and anyone interested in humour research or popular culture
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing jokes by crowd-sourced ratings to find broadly appealing humour, including cross-cultural and demographic comparisons, comparisons of human vs computer-generated jokes, and simple popularity measures (submission counts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant-rated funniness (average score)
rubrics_metrics.description: For his experiment, Richard Wiseman created a website where people could rate and submit jokes; the winning joke was the one that scored best by the aggregated ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect ratings from many participants and compute an overall average to identify the joke with the widest appeal. As Wiseman notes, the result represents the average reaction across respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-cultural and demographic appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Purposes of the research included discovering the joke that had the widest appeal and understanding among different cultures, demographics and countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare ratings across subgroups (e.g., by country, age, gender) to see which jokes appeal broadly versus those that appeal only to particular groups. Use subgroup analysis to assess 'widest appeal.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus vs subgroup preference (minimizing dislike)
rubrics_metrics.description: Richard Wiseman: 'It was the joke that most people didn't hate... when you pulled the data, you got the average.' Different groups often have jokes they find much funnier, but the global winner minimizes overall dislike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret global winners as those with broad acceptability rather than necessarily the most loved by any one group; consider measures of variance and negative reactions as well as mean score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human vs computer-generated comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers included five computer-generated jokes, four of which fared rather poorly, but one was rated higher than one third of the human jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include algorithmic/computer-generated items as controls or benchmarks. Compare their ratings to human-created jokes to evaluate machine humour quality and where it stands relative to humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission frequency / popularity (counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke that was submitted to LaughLab the most times was: 'What's brown and sticky? A stick.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track how often a joke is submitted as a measure of popularity or memetic spread; submission count may capture a different facet of 'popularity' than mean funniness ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance / originality of jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: The winning joke was later found to be based on a 1951 Goon Show sketch by Spike Milligan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify origins and prior appearances of jokes when claiming novelty or 'world's funniest' status; provenance can affect claims about originality or the interpretation of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of an open online platform (methodological/procedural criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: LaughLab was an online site that allowed people to submit and rate jokes as part of a large-scale experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments with open submission and rating mechanisms to gather large, diverse samples; be aware this method measures self-selected online participants and may bias results.
